title: Can a robot camera calibrate itself without a checkerboard, and does it know when it is wrong?
lede: research programme on target-free camera self-calibration on two real cameras: bundle adjustment with the board's geometry withheld lands within 0.15% and 0.24% of Zhang's focal length and shows the board itself bends; over 560 converged view-subset solves the spread of view angles predicts the error (ρ −0.46/−0.58), the solver's σ is about 2× too small (2.4× near the critical set, where Zhang's is 5.8×), and a 0.5% σ gate rejects 92% of bad updates but accepts only 84% of good ones; the 2× is real (rms z 2.28 against the target-free solution), and a leave-one-view-out jackknife σ is honest with no fitted factor (rms z 0.70/0.65) but ranks good and bad updates worse (AUC 0.75 against 0.91)
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) on recalibrating a camera from the features it already sees, with no target, and on whether the solver's own uncertainty is honest enough for a robot to accept or reject the update. Milestone 1 uses OpenCV's real stereo calibration photos (two cameras, 13 views each, Apache-2.0): the checkerboard corners are kept as correspondences but the board's geometry is withheld, so the 54 corners become free 3-D points. Started 30% off in focal length, bundle adjustment lands at 534.8 and 538.4 px against Zhang's 535.6 and 539.7 px (gaps 0.15% and 0.24%, under 1σ), with a reported σ 1.12× Zhang's, refuting our prediction of a 2× price for having no target. The free corners leave their best plane by 0.0077 square widths rms (0.024 at most), and the two cameras, solved separately, reconstruct the same bend (correlation 0.90; 0.91 with a second distortion term): the printed board is not flat, which a flat-board model cannot absorb (target-free reprojection error 0.26 against 0.42 px). Over 400 random subsets of 3 to 12 views the focal length's z-score against the all-view reference has rms 1.94 (95% 1.75–2.12) for 4–12 views, so the reported σ is about twice too small; Zhang's is no better (2.16). Limits: one rig and board, corners without mismatches, the reference is itself a flat-board fit, and every solve stopped on its evaluation cap. Milestone 2 fixes the solver (gauge pinned, analytic Jacobian, Levenberg–Marquardt: all 560 solves converge, at most 177 evaluations) and confirms milestone 1's rms z (1.945 against 1.944). The largest angle between the views' board normals predicts the focal error (Spearman ρ −0.46 and −0.58), and the reported σ tracks it (ρ +0.39 / +0.45) but stays about 2× too small, 2.4× on 160 near-critical subsets of near-parallel boards. There Zhang's σ is much worse (rms z 5.8) and its focal length is further off (median 1.50% against 1.09% at 4 views). A pre-registered accept gate, σf/f ≤ 0.5%, rejected 92% of updates more than 2% off but accepted only 84% of those within 1%, short of the 90/90 target; an inflation factor fitted on one camera did not transfer cleanly to the other. Milestone 3 asks whether the 2× is real and whether a robust σ fixes it. Scored against the target-free all-view solution with the nested variance, rms z is still 2.28, so the checkerboard reference is not the cause. A leave-one-view-out jackknife (3,480 re-solves) gives an honest σ with no fitted factor: rms z 0.70 and 0.65, 2σ coverage 97–99%, and 1.01 on near-critical subsets where the reported σ gives 2.34; the cluster-robust sandwich helps only on one camera. But the jackknife is very conservative at 4 views (15× the reported σ) and ranks good against bad updates worse (ROC AUC 0.75 against 0.91), so a 0.5% jackknife gate accepts only 19% of good updates: an honest error bar and a good accept statistic are different things.
